summary: Benjamin Franklin's unfinished account of his own life, written as a record for his son. It follows him from a Boston boyhood and his early reading through his move to Philadelphia, his work as a printer, the Junto discussion club, his plan for moral perfection and his public projects, and breaks off in 1758 with his mission to London on behalf of the Pennsylvania assembly. The book has four parts, written in different periods, and is one of the most influential autobiographies ever written.
context: Franklin began Part One in 1771, wrote Part Two in France in 1784 after Abel James urged him to continue, Part Three in 1788 and 1789 after returning home, and the brief Part Four as his health failed. He seems to have called it his Memoirs. It stayed unpublished in his lifetime. A French translation appeared in 1791 and the first English edition in 1793. John Bigelow published the most reliable text yet in 1868, with Part Four in English for the first time. The site carries a modern edition with a later introduction.

ideas.title: Self-improvement by plan
ideas.note: Franklin sets out a project of arriving at moral perfection, listing thirteen virtues and marking faults in a daily book.

ideas.title: The self-made man
ideas.note: The work is a model of the self-made man in American writing.

ideas.title: Useful public projects
ideas.note: With the help of the Junto he drafts proposals such as one for the Library Company of Philadelphia.
